strengths: Important and timely problem: the paper targets universal, transferable patch attacks on VLA-driven robots under black-box conditions, addressing a genuine gap since prior work (e.g., RoboticAttack [49]) assumes white-box access to the victim policy.

Well-motivated technical framework that combines several complementary ingredients: a feature-space objective with an ℓ1 deviation term and repulsive contrastive loss, a bi-level min-max scheme emulating adversarially robust surrogates without retraining VLAs, and two VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) that exploit the text→vision cross-modal structure of VLAs.

Large-scale empirical evaluation across two datasets (LIBERO, BridgeData V2), simulation and physical settings, and multiple victims (OpenVLA-oft variants fine-tuned on different suites, OpenVLA-oft-w, and reportedly π0), with the proposed method achieving substantially lower victim success rates than six baseline objectives (e.g., 5.75% vs. 41.25–69.25% simulated transfer in Tab. 1).

Ablation study (Tab. 3, Tab. 4) covering each loss component and text-probe design, plus qualitative patch-pattern analysis (Fig. 2) that supports the claim that baselines overfit to embodiment/scene cues.

A useful threat-model formalization (Definition 1, Eq. 4-5) that separates optimization and evaluation objectives and explicitly states the strict black-box protocol, which improves reproducibility of the threat setting.
weaknesses: Manuscript incompleteness materially undermines verifiability: multiple unresolved cross-references ('Appendix ??', 'Proof is in Appendix ??', 'Proposition ??'). The white-box results, the π0 transfer results, implementation details, and the proof of Proposition 1 are all relegated to a missing appendix, so key evidence supporting the paper's central claims (transfer to heterogeneous VLAs, theory) is not present in the submission.

Theoretical support is thin. Assumption 1 (exact linear alignment with bounded residual) is empirically motivated only by a single reported number (R² ≈ 0.654) with no details on how it was measured, on which model pairs, or with what variance; Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 are direct consequences of the assumption (linear algebra) and do not validate the assumption itself, weakening the 'provably persists on the target' claim in the abstract.

Ablation conclusions are weakly supported statistically. In Tab. 3, removing RUPA, PAD, or PSM changes average success rate by only 0.75–2.0 points (61.50 → 62.25/62.50/63.50); with 10 trials per task (100 rollouts) and no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, the claim that 'dropping any single module consistently weakens the attack' is not established.

The contrastive objective in Eq. 9 and its surrounding text are confusing: as written it is the standard InfoNCE that pulls (zi, z̃i) together when minimized, while the text alternates between 'Maximizing (minimizing)' and 'repulsion'; the sign/role of Lcon relative to the stated goal of pushing patched features away from clean anchors is ambiguous and needs precise restatement.

Single-surrogate limitation: all transfer results use OpenVLA-7B as the surrogate. Given the paper's framing around model-agnostic universality, evaluating the same framework with at least one other surrogate (or reporting surrogate sensitivity) would substantially strengthen the generality claim; the π0 evidence exists but is unreportable in this draft.

Some baseline cells are near-zero (e.g., 'long' task at 3–4% for several baselines in Tab. 2), indicating task-type confounds; the paper does not analyze per-task difficulty or why certain objectives collapse on particular suites, which limits interpretation of aggregate averages.

Evaluation realism concerns: patch placement sites are predetermined per suite, and the distinction between 'Simulated' and 'Physical' columns (both showing identical Benign rates) is not clearly explained; a stronger demonstration would include randomized/attacker-chosen placements and clarity on how the physical victim differs from the simulated one.

No defense or mitigation analysis is provided despite the abstract claiming the work 'establishes a strong baseline for future defenses'; a brief evaluation of a standard patch-defense or adversarial-training baseline would contextualize the threat.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: universal, black-box transferable patch attacks on VLA-driven robots are genuinely underexplored relative to white-box VLA attacks (e.g., RoboticAttack [49]), and the paper positions the threat model (surrogate-only gradient access, no victim information) clearly in Definition 1.

Strong empirical results in the main tables: on the OpenVLA-7B → OpenVLA-oft-w transfer, the proposed patch reduces average task success from 98.25% (benign) to 5.75% (simulated) and 40.25% (physical), far exceeding the transfer of the six baseline objectives (41.25–91.25%), and remains strongest in the harder OpenVLA-oft transfer (Table 2).

The method is coherently assembled: a feature-space ℓ1 + repulsive InfoNCE objective, a bi-level min-max 'robustness-augmented' procedure that emulates adversarial training of the surrogate without retraining, and two VLA-specific losses (PAD on text→vision attention increments; PSM toward probe-phrase anchors) that are sensible for instruction-conditioned policies.

The ablations (Tables 3–4) are informative: removing the feature-space objective Jtr is catastrophic (85.75% success), and the probe-phrasing study (action vs. direction vs. joint) provides actionable insight into what drives cross-model transfer.
The patch pattern analysis (Fig. 2) gives a plausible qualitative explanation for why the learned patch is more universal than baseline patches, which mimic gripper/object cues.
weaknesses: The manuscript is visibly incomplete: multiple central cross-references are broken ('Appendix ??', 'Proposition ??', 'Proof is in Appendix ??'), and the white-box results, the π0 transfer results, and additional ablations — all of which support headline claims ('first cross-architecture transfer', 'strong white-box capability', 'physical executions') — are relegated to a missing appendix. As submitted, the evidence for several key claims cannot be verified.

The 'transfer across architectures' claim is weakly supported in the main text. Tables 1–2 transfer from OpenVLA-7B to OpenVLA-oft variants, which share the same backbone and pretraining; the genuinely heterogeneous case (π0, a flow-based policy with a different backbone) is only mentioned as appearing in the missing appendix. The cross-architecture story is thus essentially unevidenced in the submitted manuscript.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Assumption 1 (linear alignment with bounded residual) is strong and largely unverified — the only evidence is an R² ≈ 0.654 CCA/probe claim with no experimental details, and σmin(A⋆) is never estimated for the actual surrogate–victim pair. Proposition 1 is a direct consequence of the assumption, so the 'provably persistent deviations' framing oversells what is essentially a linear-alignment heuristic.

Terminology around 'physical' is confusing and possibly overstated: the abstract claims 'physical executions', but Tables 1–2 appear to compare patches trained/evaluated with a simulation-trained model (LIBERO) versus a model trained on real-world BridgeData V2 — both evaluated in LIBERO rollouts (the 'Benign' rows are identical across the Simulated and Physical columns). It is unclear whether any real robot was ever attacked; the paper should state this unambiguously.

The threat model contains a favorable assumption: 'patch placement sites are predetermined for each suite to avoid occluding objects in the test scenes' (Sec. 4.1). A universal patch in a realistic deployment cannot rely on curated placement, so reported success rates may overstate practical risk.

Ablation evidence for the headline components is marginal: w/o RUPA (62.25 vs. 61.50), w/o PAD (62.50), w/o PSM (63.50), and w/o L1 (64.00) differ from the full model by roughly 1–3 points with 100 rollouts per suite and no error bars or significance testing. Almost all of the gain comes from the generic feature-space objective Jtr, which weakens the case that the VLA-specific losses (PAD, PSM) and the bi-level procedure are the key contributions.

The baseline set is narrow: only the six objectives from RoboticAttack [49] are compared. Standard transferability techniques from the patch/classifier literature that the paper itself cites (input diversity [56], translation invariance [13], feature disruption [16]) are not evaluated as patch-attack baselines, so it is hard to attribute the gains to the VLA-specific design rather than to generic training recipes.

Relation to closely related concurrent work is insufficiently discussed: [57] (model-agnostic adversarial attack and defense for VLAs) and [63] (BadVLA, objective-decoupled optimization) appear to overlap in motivation, but differences in setting and method are not articulated.

Several writing/consistency issues: Eq. 10 defines the weight as λ but the text says λ_con; 'adversarially trained large VLA policies is practically prohibitive'; the claim that InfoNCE 'concentrates the change along directions that are consistently shared across the batch' is asserted rather than demonstrated (no CCA analysis of the resulting displacement directions).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable adversarial patches against VLA-driven robots under black-box conditions. Prior work (RoboticAttack [49]) assumes white-box access, so the transfer setting is a meaningful step for safety assessment.

The method is well-motivated: the CCA/linear-probe analysis (R2 ≈ 0.654, near-unity top canonical correlations) provides empirical justification for learning patches in a shared feature space, and the derived Proposition 1 gives a clean (if simple) link between surrogate-side ℓ1 deviation and target-side response.

The two VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) are thoughtfully designed and grounded in the actual structure of VLA policies (text→vision attention to action-relevant queries, instruction conditioning), which is more than a generic feature-space attack.

Empirically, the results are strong and consistent: 5.75% vs. 41.25–69.25% average success for baselines in simulated transfer (Tab. 1) and 40.25% vs. 65.00–91.25% in the physical setting, with ablations (Tab. 3, 4) probing each component and the probe-phrasing design.

The patch pattern analysis (Fig. 2) offers an interesting qualitative insight: baselines learn scene-tied, embodiment-mimicking textures while the proposed patch learns model-agnostic patterns, which plausibly explains the transfer gap.
weaknesses: The manuscript is not submission-ready: multiple broken references ('Proof is in Appendix ??', 'The results in Appendix ??', 'Additional transfer results ... in Appendix ??', 'More implementation details can be found in the Appendix ??'). The white-box results, π0 transfer numbers, and key hyperparameters are all deferred to a missing appendix, making the central claims (including the stringent π0 transfer) unverifiable from the provided material.

The headline 'robustness-augmented' contribution (RUPA) is barely supported by the ablation: w/o RUPA yields 62.25% vs. 61.50% for the full method (Tab. 3), a difference of 0.75 points that is likely within noise given only 100 rollouts per suite and no variance/std reporting. Similarly, w/o PAD (62.50) and w/o PSM (63.50) contribute little; nearly all of the gain comes from the feature-space objective Jtr. The contribution list and the ablation evidence are therefore mismatched.

The experimental semantics of 'Simulated' vs. 'Physical' columns in Tabs. 1 and 2 are confusing: the victim (OpenVLA-oft-w on LIBERO) is a simulation-trained model, yet a 'Physical' column is reported. The text suggests this refers to the data the surrogate/patch was trained on, but the protocol is never clearly defined, which undermines interpretation of the sim-to-real claims.

Transfer diversity is limited. All quantitative main results (Tabs. 1–4) transfer from a single surrogate (OpenVLA-7B) to victims within the same family (OpenVLA-oft variants) that share the DINOv2+SigLIP vision encoder and overall architecture; the cross-family π0 transfer — the strongest test of the 'model-agnostic' claim — is relegated to a broken appendix reference with no numbers in the main text.

The strict black-box claim is softened by the evaluation protocol: 'patch placement sites are predetermined for each suite to avoid occluding objects in the test scenes', implying attacker knowledge of scene layout, which a real attacker would not have.

Assumption 1 (linear alignment with bounded residual) is strong and somewhat circular: the paper empirically observes R2 ≈ 0.654, which is moderate, yet the theory assumes near-invertible linear alignment with small residual; the bound in Prop. 1 is also a direct consequence of the assumption. The proof is missing (Appendix ??), so the theoretical contribution cannot be assessed.

Despite framing the work as 'establishing a strong baseline for future defenses', no defense evaluation or robustness analysis is included (e.g., patch localization, adversarial training on the victim, or sensitivity to patch scale/material).

No code or reproducibility statement is evident, and with broken appendix references plus many unspecified hyperparameters (λcon, λPAD, λPSM, ϵσ, I, K, patch size, etc.) in the main text, reproduction would be difficult.

Writing quality is below CVPR bar in places (e.g., 'an optimiz-ing loss', 'adversarially trained large VLA policies is', 'π0 which provide'), and Algorithm 1's placement of the inner/outer loops inside the mini-batch loop leaves ambiguous whether σ⋆ is re-solved per batch or reused.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: universal, transferable adversarial patches for VLA-driven robots under black-box conditions, which existing patch attacks (e.g., RoboticAttack [57]) do not cover since they assume white-box access to the victim.

The proposed framework (UPA-RFAS) is well-structured and reasonably novel, combining a feature-space ℓ1 + repulsive InfoNCE objective, a two-phase robustness-augmented (RAUP) min-max procedure, and two VLA-specific losses (PAD for attention hijacking, PSM for semantic misalignment) that are tailored to the text→vision cross-modal structure of VLAs.

Main results (Tab. 1) show large improvements over six baseline objectives: transferring OpenVLA-7B to OpenVLA-oft-w reduces average success rate from 98.25% benign to 5.75% in simulation and 40.25% in the physical-trained setting, versus 41.25–69.25% for baselines.

Substantial ablations support the design: component-wise removal (Tab. 2), probe-phrase composition (Tab. 3), patch size, λ_con, and ε for RUPA (Tabs. 6–8), plus qualitative analysis of patch patterns explaining why baselines overfit to scene-tied cues (Fig. 2).

A theoretical justification (Prop. 1, Cor. 1) links surrogate-side feature deviation to target-side deviation under a linear alignment assumption, and the CCA/probing analysis (R²≈0.654) gives empirical motivation for the shared-subspace premise.

The evaluation spans multiple victim variants (OpenVLA-oft fine-tuned on four suites plus a multi-suite model), white-box results, π0 transfer, and qualitative real-robot executions with supplementary videos, strengthening reproducibility of the threat analysis.
weaknesses: The 'black-box transfer' claim is partially weakened by the choice of victims: OpenVLA-oft is built directly on OpenVLA and shares its vision backbone, so the main results (Tab. 1) largely demonstrate cross-recipe/cross-task transfer within one model family. Transfer to a genuinely different architecture (π0, Appendix D) is modest: success drops only from 92.0% to 86.0% (simulated) and 89.0% to 83.5% (physical), with the best baseline (UADA1 88.5%) only 2.5 points behind — a margin that may be within noise for 100 rollouts, and no variance estimates are reported for the main tables.

The 'Simulated vs. Physical' column semantics in Tab. 1 are confusing: 'physical' appears to denote a victim trained on real-world BridgeData V2 data, yet evaluation still appears to run in the LIBERO simulator. The genuinely real-world evaluation (Appendix F) is only qualitative (3 tasks × 3 trials), so sim-to-real robustness is not quantitatively established despite being a headline claim.

Assumption 1 (a full-rank linear map between surrogate and target feature spaces with bounded residual) is strong; the theory reduces to a reverse-triangle-inequality argument, and the connection from feature displacement to actual policy failure (action head behavior) is not formally addressed — the ℓ1 lower bound does not by itself explain the observed task-success degradation.

The threat model has favorable assumptions that are not fully discussed: patch placement sites are 'predetermined for each suite to avoid occluding objects' (i.e., the attacker knows safe locations in advance), and the attacker has access to training data Ds from the surrogate's domain.

The white-box results (Tab. 4) contain anomalies that raise questions about evaluation protocol: baselines UMA/UADA reduce success to 0–0.5% in simulation while the paper's method averages 0.5%, yet 'physical' white-box numbers show much weaker baselines (e.g., UMA1 at 26.2%) for the same nominal white-box setup — the difference between simulated/physical conditions under white-box access needs clearer explanation.

Several presentation issues impede reproducibility: the code link is empty ('Code is at .'), notation is inconsistent (Eq. 10 introduces 'λ > 0' while later text and Algorithm 1 use λ_con; PAD's λ_non appears only in the appendix), and the direction of optimization for the InfoNCE repulsion is described confusingly ('Maximizing (minimizing) L_con encourages the similarity to decrease (increase)').

Missing statistical rigor in the headline tables (no confidence intervals or seeds), and some ablation trends (e.g., w/o RUPA at 62.25 vs. full 61.50, a 0.75-point difference) are too small to conclusively attribute importance to individual components.

Robustness of conclusions across transfer targets is uneven: the paper's strong advantage over baselines holds on OpenVLA-oft variants but nearly vanishes on π0, which should temper the claim of 'consistently transfers across models.'

strengths: Timely and safety-relevant problem: universal, transferable patch attacks against VLA-driven robots in a black-box threat model are indeed underexplored, and the paper is, to my knowledge, among the first to formalize this setting (Definition 1 separates surrogate-side optimization from victim-side evaluation).

The strongest empirical result is convincing: on OpenVLA-7B → OpenVLA-oft-w transfer (Table 1), the proposed patch reduces simulated task success from 98.25% (benign) to 5.75%, while the RoboticAttack baselines remain at 41.25–69.25%; the physical-setting trend (40.25% vs. 65.00–91.25% for baselines) is consistent. This is a clear, quantified improvement over existing VLA patch objectives in the cross-recipe regime.

The method is a coherent composition of known and new ideas: ℓ1 feature deviation with a linear-alignment justification (Prop. 1), repulsive InfoNCE, a bi-level RAUP scheme emulating robust surrogates without retraining a VLA, and two VLA-specific losses (PAD on text→vision attention increments; PSM with probe-phrase anchors).

Ablations are reasonably thorough (component ablation in Table 2, probe phrasing in Table 3, patch size / λ_con / ε in Appendix E), and the white-box results (Appendix C) show the objective is not merely a transferability trick.
The patch-pattern analysis (Fig. 2) provides a plausible qualitative account of why baseline patches overfit to scene/embodiment cues while the proposed patch does not.
weaknesses: Cross-architecture transfer—the setting the paper itself identifies as the motivation—is only weakly supported. On π0 (Table 5), the attack reduces success from 92.00% to 86.00% simulated and 92.00% to 83.50% physical, only 2.5–5.5 points below the best baseline, and several baselines (e.g., UMA_1 at 89.25/93.50) are at or above benign performance. The main text claim that results 'show that our methods still enhance attacks in the most challenging case' overstates a marginal effect, and the abstract's 'consistently transfers across models' does not hold for the only genuinely heterogeneous victim.

The real-world evidence is thin given the paper's framing. Appendix F reports only 3 tasks × 3 trials, purely qualitative, with no success-rate numbers, no baselines in the physical setup, and no statistical treatment—yet the title and abstract lead with physical robotic attacks. Section 4.1's 'physical setting' appears to be a model trained on BridgeData V2, evaluated in simulation, which conflates 'physical data' with 'physical deployment'.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the experimental protocol. Section 4.1 states transfer is evaluated to 'four different OpenVLA-oft variants' fine-tuned on distinct suites, but Table 1 reports only two victims (OpenVLA-oft-w and OpenVLA-oft). Benign success is 98.25% in Table 1 but 76.5% in the white-box Table 4, and the victim/surrogate configurations across tables are not always clearly disambiguated. In Table 5, UMA_1 attains 93.50% physical success vs. 92.00% benign—an attack improving task success—which suggests measurement noise or protocol issues that go unexamined.

The theoretical component is cosmetic. Assumption 1 (a globally linear map between encoder outputs with bounded residual) is strong and only moderately supported (R² ≈ 0.654, i.e., ~35% of target variance unexplained); Proposition 1 is a direct application of the singular-value inequality plus reverse triangle inequality, and the ε_E residual term is never estimated or validated. The theory does not actually predict the observed transfer behavior nor inform any design decision beyond motivating an ℓ1 loss.

The method is a heavy stack of components (ℓ1 + InfoNCE + RAUP bi-level loop + PAD + PSM) with many hyperparameters (λ_con=10, λ_PAD=1, λ_PSM=0.5, m=0.1, top-ρ=0.3, two temperatures, etc.), and component ablations show surprisingly small individual effects (w/o RUPA 62.25, w/o PAD 62.50, w/o PSM 63.50 vs. 61.50 full). Much of the gain comes from the feature-space stage (w/o J_tr = 85.75); it remains unclear whether the VLA-specific PAD/PSM losses justify their complexity.

Notation and presentation issues: ρ is used both for the patch area budget (Eq. 1) and the TopK attention fraction (Eq. 14); Eq. 20 is referenced in Algorithm 1 before J_out is defined; the 'Maximizing (minimizing)' sentence around Eq. 9 is confusing; Eq. 17's notation (norm applied to a vector expression) is ambiguous. The code URL in the abstract is empty, so reproducibility currently rests entirely on Appendix B.

The evaluation is restricted to OpenVLA-derived victims plus one π0 transfer; no defense baselines are evaluated despite the paper framing itself as 'a strong baseline for future defenses'—the defensive value of the study is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and safety-relevant problem: universal and transferable adversarial patch attacks on VLA-driven robots under black-box conditions. Existing patch attacks on VLAs (e.g., RoboticAttack [57]) assume white-box access and co-adapt to a single model, so the transferability framing is a meaningful advance in threat modeling for embodied AI.

The method is well-constructed and combines principled components: an ℓ1 feature-deviation objective with a repulsive InfoNCE term, a bi-level robustness-augmented optimization (RUPA) that emulates robust surrogates without retraining large VLAs, and two VLA-specific losses (PAD exploiting text→vision attention, PSM exploiting instruction-embedding mismatch). Each component is clearly motivated.

The empirical evaluation is broad and follows a strict transfer protocol: surrogate OpenVLA-7B to OpenVLA-oft variants fine-tuned on different LIBERO suites, a jointly-trained multi-suite model, and the architecturally dissimilar π0, plus sim-to-real and physical deployment settings. Table 1 shows large degradations (98.25% → 5.75% simulated, 40.25% physical) far below all six baselines, which is a convincing headline result.

Useful ablations (Table 2, 3, 6-8) demonstrate that each module contributes, reveal an interpretable direction-vs-magnitude division of labor between L_con and L_1, and characterize sensitivity to patch size and perturbation budget. The patch pattern analysis (Fig. 2) offers an interesting qualitative explanation of why baseline patches overfit to scene-specific cues while the proposed patch does not.
The paper is generally well-written, the problem formulation (Eq. 1-5) is clean, and implementation details (Appendix B) plus supplementary videos support reproducibility; code release is promised.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and somewhat overstated. Proposition 1 is a direct consequence of a singular-value inequality under Assumption 1, and the abstract/intro language ('provably persist on the target') is stronger than warranted: ε_E is never measured, σ_min(A*) is never estimated, and the empirical evidence (R² ≈ 0.654, i.e., roughly 35% of target variance unexplained by the linear map) only partially supports the linear-alignment premise. The theory justifies the ℓ1 term post hoc rather than predicting behavior.

The π0 results (Table 5) are much weaker than the headline narrative suggests: simulated average drops only from 92.0% to 86.0%, just 2.5 points below the best baseline (88.5%), and the physical result (83.5% vs. 89.0%) is a modest margin. With no variance or significance testing reported for Tables 1 and 5 (100 rollouts per suite), several baseline-vs-method gaps, particularly for π0, could be within run-to-run noise. Only the white-box appendix reports standard deviations.

The causal mechanism is asserted rather than verified on victims. PAD and PSM are motivated by attention hijacking and semantic misalignment, but the paper never shows that attention actually shifts to the patch on the victim models, or that the semantic anchoring produces the claimed image-text mismatch there; Fig. 2 analyzes patch appearance, not mechanism. The ablations show the components help but not why.

Real-world evaluation is only qualitative: three tasks × three trials, no success-rate numbers, no statistical support, and no comparison against baselines in the physical setup. Given that sim-to-real transfer is a central claim, this is a limited evidence base.

Some presentational issues create ambiguity: ρ denotes both the patch area budget (Eq. 1) and the top-ρ text-token ratio (Eq. 14); Table 1's column layout ('Simulated/Physical' under two victim labels) does not exactly match the textual description of which victim corresponds to which setting; the 'w/o J_tr' ablation conflates removing RUPA's inner loop with removing the feature objective, making attribution between RUPA and the feature losses partly confounded.

Patch placement sites are predetermined per suite to avoid occluding objects, and the ablation (Table 6) shows attack strength rises sharply with patch size (79.75% success at 3% vs. 20.75% at 10%), so part of the reported degradation may reflect patch footprint and placement convenience rather than the proposed objectives; a placement-randomized or defense-aware evaluation would strengthen the threat-model claim.

No discussion of defenses (even simple input transformations or patch detection), limited ethical/dual-use discussion for a physical-robot attack paper, and no comparison against simpler transferability tricks (e.g., EOT-only, input diversity baselines) to isolate what RUPA and the VLA-specific losses add beyond standard augmentation.
